title: Breathing, Gas Exchange and Diffusion in the Lungs
kicker: Cambridge Lower Secondary · Science 0893 · Stage 8 · Biology
summary: How the lungs, ribs, intercostal muscles and diaphragm move air, how oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse in the alveoli, and why breathing is not the same as respiration — with Checkpoint-style practice.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Describe how the structure of the respiratory system (the lungs, the diaphragm and the intercostal muscles) helps it do its job of gas exchange (8Bs.03)
Explain the difference between breathing and respiration (8Bs.03)
Describe how oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse between the blood and the air in the lungs (8Bs.04)

blocks.text: Every cell in your body needs **oxygen** for respiration, and every cell makes **carbon dioxide** as a waste product. Your **respiratory system** brings oxygen into the body and removes carbon dioxide. On this page you will learn how the parts of the system are built for this job, how muscles make you breathe, and how gases cross from the air into the blood by **diffusion**.

items: respiratory system
الجهاز التنفسي — the organs that bring air into the body and carry out gas exchange
trachea (windpipe)
القصبة الهوائية — the tube from the throat to the lungs

الشُّعبة الهوائية — one of the two tubes that branch from the trachea into the lungs
bronchiole
الشُّعيبة الهوائية — a very small tube that branches from a bronchus
alveolus (plural alveoli)
الحويصلة الهوائية — a tiny air sac where gas exchange happens
diaphragm
الحجاب الحاجز — a sheet of muscle under the lungs
intercostal muscles
العضلات الوربية (بين الضلوع) — muscles between the ribs
gas exchange
تبادل الغازات — oxygen goes into the blood and carbon dioxide comes out

الانتشار — particles spreading from where there are many (high concentration) to where there are few (low concentration)

blocks.text: The parts of the respiratory system

When you breathe in, air travels along this route: **nose or mouth → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli**. The lungs sit inside the chest (the **thorax**), protected by the **ribs**. Underneath the lungs is the **diaphragm**, which separates the chest from the abdomen.

headers: How the structure helps its function
rows: Hairs and a moist, sticky lining
Traps dust; warms and moistens the air before it reaches the lungs
A wide tube held open by **rings of cartilage**; lined with **mucus** and tiny hairs called **cilia**
The rings stop it collapsing, so air can always pass. Mucus traps dust and microorganisms; cilia sweep the mucus up to the throat
Tubes that branch again and again, like the branches of a tree
Carry air to every part of both lungs
Millions of tiny air sacs with very thin walls, each covered in **capillaries**
This is where **gas exchange** happens (see below)
Bones that form a cage around the lungs
Protect the lungs and heart; move up and out to make the chest bigger
Contract to pull the ribs up and out when you breathe in
A dome-shaped sheet of muscle under the lungs
Contracts and flattens to make the chest bigger when you breathe in

blocks.text: **Exam vocabulary:** say **bronchus** for one tube and **bronchi** for two; **alveolus** for one air sac and **alveoli** for many. Checkpoint mark schemes usually accept phonetic spellings, but learn the correct ones.
Breathing: how muscles move air

Your lungs have no muscles of their own. They are moved by the **diaphragm** and the **intercostal muscles**. The idea that explains breathing is about **volume and pressure**: when the volume inside the chest gets **bigger**, the air pressure inside the lungs becomes **lower** than the air pressure outside, so air is pushed **in**. When the volume gets **smaller**, the pressure inside becomes **higher** than outside, so air is pushed **out**. (Air always moves from higher pressure to lower pressure.)

rows: **relaxes** and goes back to a **dome** (moves up)

items: To describe breathing IN, write the steps in this order: muscles contract → ribs up and out / diaphragm flattens → volume of chest increases → pressure decreases → air moves in.
To describe breathing OUT, reverse every step: muscles relax → ribs down and in / diaphragm domes up → volume decreases → pressure increases → air moves out.

blocks.text: **Try it:** put your hands on your ribs and breathe in deeply. You can feel your ribs move up and out. Put a hand on your stomach: it moves out a little because the flattened diaphragm pushes down on the organs below.
A model of breathing: the bell jar
Scientists use **models** to show ideas we cannot easily see. The bell jar model is an **analogy**: each part of the model stands for a part of the body.

headers: Limitations (where the model is not like the body)
rows: Pulling the sheet down (like the diaphragm flattening) increases the volume inside the jar, so the pressure falls and air goes into the balloons
The glass jar cannot move, but real **ribs move** up and out — the model has **no intercostal muscles**
Letting the sheet go back reduces the volume, so air leaves the balloons
The real diaphragm is a muscle that **contracts**; the sheet is pulled by a hand from outside
The balloons fill and empty with air, like lungs
Balloons are hollow bags; real lungs are spongy with millions of **alveoli** and there is **no gas exchange** in the model

blocks.title: الشهيق والزفير بالعربي
blocks.text: في الشهيق: العضلات اللي بين الضلوع بتنقبض فالضلوع تطلع لفوق ولبرّه، والحجاب الحاجز ينقبض ويبقى مفرود (ينزل لتحت). حجم الصدر يكبر ← الضغط جواه يقل ← الهوا يدخل. في الزفير بيحصل العكس بالظبط: العضلات ترتخي، الضلوع تنزل، الحجاب يرجع على شكل قبة، الحجم يصغر ← الضغط يزيد ← الهوا يخرج. احفظ السلسلة دي بالترتيب: عضلات ← حجم ← ضغط ← هوا.
Gas exchange in the alveoli

Each bronchiole ends in a bunch of tiny air sacs called **alveoli**. Each alveolus is wrapped in a net of **capillaries** (the smallest blood vessels). This is where **gas exchange** happens. It happens by **diffusion**: particles of a gas move from a place where they are in **high concentration** to a place where they are in **low concentration**. No muscles or energy are needed; the particles move by themselves because they are always moving randomly.

blocks.caption: One alveolus and a capillary (much simplified). Oxygen diffuses from the air into the blood; carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the air.

items: Blood arriving at the lungs from the body has **little oxygen** and **a lot of carbon dioxide** (the cells used the oxygen and made carbon dioxide in respiration).
The air in the alveolus has **a lot of oxygen** (fresh air was just breathed in) and **little carbon dioxide**.
**Oxygen** diffuses from the air in the alveolus, through the alveolus wall and the capillary wall, **into the blood**. It is carried by the **red blood cells**.
**Carbon dioxide** diffuses the other way: from the blood (mostly the **plasma**) **into the air** in the alveolus. It is then breathed out.
The blood, now rich in oxygen, flows back to the heart, which pumps it to the rest of the body.

blocks.text: Why the alveoli are so good at gas exchange

rows: **Very large surface area** — hundreds of millions of alveoli; spread out flat they would cover about 70 m^{2}, more than the floor of a classroom
More gas can diffuse at the same time
**Very thin walls** — the alveolus wall and the capillary wall are each only **one cell thick**
**Short distance** for the gases to diffuse, so it is fast
Oxygen **dissolves** in the moisture first, then diffuses through the wall
**Good blood supply** — a dense network of capillaries; the blood keeps flowing
Oxygen-rich blood is carried away at once and new low-oxygen blood arrives, so the difference in concentration stays **large** (a steep **concentration gradient**)
Keeps the oxygen concentration in the alveoli high and the carbon dioxide low

blocks.text: **Exam technique:** for "explain how the alveoli are adapted", always link the **feature** to **why it helps**: "the walls are one cell thick, **so** the diffusion distance is short". A feature on its own usually earns only half the credit.
Inhaled air and exhaled air
Because of gas exchange, the air you breathe out is different from the air you breathe in. These are typical values:

rows: The body does not use nitrogen
Oxygen diffused into the blood for respiration
Carbon dioxide from respiration diffused out of the blood
Water evaporates from the moist lining of the alveoli

blocks.text: Notice that exhaled air still contains a lot of oxygen (about 16%). That is why rescue breaths in first aid can help someone who has stopped breathing. You can show that exhaled air has more carbon dioxide with **limewater**: it turns **milky (cloudy)** much faster when you breathe out through it than when inhaled air is bubbled through it.
Breathing is NOT respiration

rows: Muscles move **air** into and out of the lungs
Gases **diffuse** between the air in the alveoli and the blood
A **chemical reaction** that **releases energy** from glucose
Chemical reaction: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water

blocks.text: Breathing and gas exchange **supply** the oxygen that respiration needs and **remove** the carbon dioxide it makes. Plants respire too, but they do not breathe. You will study respiration fully on the Aerobic Respiration page.

blocks.title: الفرق المهم
blocks.text: Breathing (التنفس/التهوية) = حركة الهوا داخل وخارج الرئتين بالعضلات. Respiration (التنفس الخلوي) = تفاعل كيميائي جوه كل خلية بيطلّع طاقة من الجلوكوز. وتبادل الغازات بيحصل في الحويصلات الهوائية بالانتشار: الأكسجين من الهوا للدم، وثاني أكسيد الكربون من الدم للهوا — دايماً من التركيز العالي للتركيز القليل.
Worked examples

**Worked example 1** (the route of air)
Describe the route taken by air from the nose to the place where gas exchange happens. [2]

items: nose → **trachea** → **bronchus / bronchi** → **bronchioles** → **alveoli**
1 mark for the correct structures, 1 mark for the correct order. Ending at the alveoli is essential — "lungs" alone is too vague.
**Common mistake:** putting bronchioles before bronchi. Big tubes come first: trachea, then bronchi, then the small bronchioles.

blocks.text:
**Worked example 2** (explaining inhaling)
Explain how the intercostal muscles and the diaphragm make air move into the lungs. [4]

items: The **intercostal muscles contract** and pull the ribs **up and out**. [1]
The **diaphragm contracts** and **flattens** (moves down). [1]
This **increases the volume** inside the chest. [1]
So the **pressure** inside the lungs **decreases** (becomes lower than outside) and air is pushed into the lungs. [1]
**Common mistake:** "the lungs suck air in" or "the air goes in, so the chest gets bigger". The muscles act first; the air moves because of the pressure change.

blocks.text:
**Worked example 3** (calculation)
At rest, Karim takes 15 breaths per minute. Each breath moves 0.5 litres of air into his lungs.
(a) Calculate the volume of air he breathes in each minute. [1]
(b) During a race his breathing rate rises to 40 breaths per minute and each breath is 2.0 litres. Calculate how many times more air per minute he breathes during the race. [2]

items: (a) 15 × 0.5 = **7.5 litres per minute**
(b) During the race: 40 × 2.0 = 80 litres per minute. 80 ÷ 7.5 = **10.7 times** (to 1 decimal place). [1 for 80, 1 for the answer; ecf from (a)]
**Exam technique:** write the units at each step and show the calculation, so you can still score if one number is wrong.

blocks.text:
**Worked example 4** (gas exchange)
Explain how oxygen gets from the air in an alveolus into the blood. Use the idea of concentration in your answer. [3]

items: The concentration of oxygen is **higher in the alveolus** than in the blood. [1]
Oxygen **diffuses** from high to low concentration, through the **thin walls** of the alveolus and capillary (one cell thick). [1]
It enters the blood and is carried by **red blood cells**; the blood flows away, so the concentration in the blood stays low. [1]
**Common mistake:** writing "oxygen is pumped into the blood". Diffusion needs no pump.

blocks.text:
**Worked example 5** (breathing and respiration)
Salma says, "Breathing and respiration are the same thing." Explain why she is wrong. [2]

items: Breathing is the **movement of air** into and out of the lungs (caused by muscles). [1]
Respiration is a **chemical reaction** in **cells** that **releases energy** from glucose (using oxygen). [1]
**Common mistake:** saying "respiration happens in the lungs". It happens in every cell, including the cells of the lungs.

blocks.text:
**Worked example 6** (evaluating a model)
The bell jar model is used to show breathing. Give two ways the model is different from the real chest. [2]

items: Any two: the jar wall is **rigid** but ribs **move** / there are **no intercostal muscles** / the rubber sheet is **pulled by hand** but the diaphragm **contracts** / balloons are **hollow** but lungs are spongy with **alveoli** / **no gas exchange** happens in the model.
**Exam technique:** compare both sides — "the jar … but the ribs …". A difference must say what the real body does.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Mixing up breathing and respiration. Breathing = moving air; respiration = releasing energy in cells.
Saying the diaphragm moves **up** when you breathe in. It **contracts and flattens**, moving **down**.
Writing that the lungs inflate first and that makes the chest bigger. The muscles make the chest bigger first; then air moves in.
Getting pressure backwards: bigger volume → **lower** pressure → air **in**.
Saying exhaled air has no oxygen. It still has about 16% oxygen.
Writing "the alveoli have thin walls" without explaining **so the diffusion distance is short**.
Saying gases diffuse from low to high concentration. Diffusion is always from **high to low**.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: **Label a diagram** of the lungs with letters (trachea, bronchus, bronchiole, alveoli, rib, diaphragm). Read the leader lines carefully.
**Complete sentences** with missing words such as contract / relax, increases / decreases, up / down.
**Explain** questions worth 3–4 marks: write one idea per line in a logical chain (muscles → volume → pressure → air).
**Data**: a table comparing inhaled and exhaled air, or a graph of lung volume over time. You may be asked to calculate a difference, a breathing rate or the volume per minute.
**Models**: say what each part of a model represents and give its limitations (an analogy, 8TWSm.01).
Use the key words exactly: **diffusion**, **concentration**, **alveoli**, **capillaries**, **surface area**.

blocks.title: Breathing and gas exchange: practice
blocks.intro: 14 Checkpoint-style questions, from easy to hard. Check your answers, then read the full solutions.

questions.q: Which shows the correct route of air into the lungs?
c: mouth → bronchi → trachea → alveoli → bronchioles
mouth → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli
mouth → trachea → bronchioles → bronchi → alveoli
mouth → alveoli → bronchioles → bronchi → trachea
questions.e: Air passes down the trachea, which splits into two bronchi; these branch into bronchioles, which end in the alveoli.

questions.q: Name the dome-shaped sheet of muscle under the lungs.
questions.e: The diaphragm separates the chest from the abdomen. It contracts and flattens when you breathe in.

questions.q: What happens to the diaphragm when you breathe in?
c: It relaxes and moves up into a dome
It relaxes and moves down
It contracts and flattens
It contracts and moves up into a dome
questions.e: When you breathe in, the diaphragm muscle contracts. This makes it flatten (move down), so the volume of the chest increases.

questions.q: Which statement about breathing and respiration is correct?
c: Respiration releases energy in cells; breathing moves air into and out of the lungs.
Breathing releases energy; respiration moves air.
Respiration happens only in the lungs.
Plants breathe but do not respire.
questions.e: Respiration is a chemical reaction in every living cell that releases energy from glucose. Breathing is the movement of air. Plants respire all the time but do not breathe.

questions.q: Name the tiny air sacs in the lungs where gas exchange happens.
questions.e: Gas exchange happens in the alveoli (one: alveolus), which are surrounded by capillaries.

questions.q: The walls of the alveoli are only one cell thick. Why does this help gas exchange?
c: It makes the lungs lighter
It stops dust getting into the blood
It gives the lungs a larger volume
It gives a short distance for the gases to diffuse
questions.e: A thin wall means a short diffusion distance, so oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse across quickly.

questions.q: Explain why carbon dioxide moves from the blood into the alveoli. [2]
questions.ms: 1 mark: the concentration of carbon dioxide is higher in the blood than in the air in the alveoli (accept: blood from the body has a lot of CO2 made by respiration). 1 mark: it diffuses from high to low concentration (across the thin walls). Do not accept 'it is pumped' or 'the blood pushes it out'.
questions.e: Blood coming from the body carries a lot of carbon dioxide made by respiration in the cells. The air in the alveoli has very little carbon dioxide. So carbon dioxide diffuses from the higher concentration in the blood to the lower concentration in the alveoli, then it is breathed out.

questions.p:
Question 9
Inhaled air contains about 0.04% carbon dioxide. Exhaled air contains about 4% carbon dioxide.
questions.q: How many times greater is the percentage of carbon dioxide in exhaled air?
questions.e: 4 ÷ 0.04 = 100. Exhaled air has about 100 times more carbon dioxide than inhaled air.

questions.p:
Question 10
A teacher uses a bell jar model with two balloons, a Y-shaped glass tube and a rubber sheet at the bottom.
questions.q: (a) Which part of the body does the rubber sheet represent?
questions.e: Pulling the rubber sheet down is like the diaphragm contracting and flattening.

questions.p:
Question 10
A teacher uses a bell jar model with two balloons, a Y-shaped glass tube and a rubber sheet at the bottom.
questions.q: (b) Give one limitation of the bell jar model and explain what happens in the real body instead. [2]
questions.ms: 1 mark for a limitation, 1 mark for what really happens. E.g. jar/sides cannot move (1), real ribs move up and out / there are intercostal muscles (1); OR sheet pulled by a hand (1), the diaphragm is a muscle that contracts (1); OR balloons are hollow (1), real lungs are spongy with alveoli / gas exchange happens (1).
questions.e: Example answer: the walls of the bell jar are rigid and cannot move, but in the real body the intercostal muscles move the ribs up and out, which also increases the volume of the chest.

questions.q: Which describes what happens when you breathe out?
c: Ribs move down and in; chest volume decreases; pressure in the lungs increases
Ribs move up and out; chest volume increases; pressure in the lungs decreases
Ribs move down and in; chest volume increases; pressure in the lungs increases
Ribs move up and out; chest volume decreases; pressure in the lungs decreases
questions.e: Breathing out: intercostal muscles and diaphragm relax, ribs go down and in, the diaphragm domes up, the volume decreases, so the pressure inside increases and air is pushed out.

questions.p:
Question 12
In one lung disease, the thin walls between many alveoli break down. The lungs then have fewer, larger air spaces.
questions.q: Explain why a person with this disease gets out of breath very easily. [3]
questions.ms: 1 mark: the surface area (for gas exchange) is smaller. 1 mark: so less oxygen diffuses into the blood (per minute). 1 mark: so the cells get less oxygen for respiration / less energy is released, so the person breathes faster to try to get enough oxygen. Accept: less carbon dioxide removed.
questions.e: Fewer, larger air spaces have a much smaller total surface area. Less oxygen can diffuse into the blood each minute, so the body cells receive less oxygen for respiration and release less energy. The person breathes faster and deeper to try to get enough oxygen, so they feel out of breath.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Route of air: nose/mouth → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.
Breathing in: intercostal muscles and diaphragm **contract** → ribs up and out, diaphragm flattens → volume ↑ → pressure ↓ → air in. Breathing out is the reverse.
Gas exchange happens in the alveoli by **diffusion**: oxygen from air into blood, carbon dioxide from blood into air — always high to low concentration.
Alveoli are adapted by: huge surface area, walls one cell thick (short distance), moist lining, rich blood supply (keeps the concentration gradient).
Breathing moves air; respiration is a chemical reaction in every cell that releases energy.
